workflow_activities.action: Count components and connections and use directed-path reachability to determine independent functional groups and cyclomatic numbers at subsystem and system levels.

workflow_activities.decision_rules: Components connected by a directed path in either direction are classified in the same functional group.

inputs: Basic COCOMO parameters a = 3.6 and b = 1.20

workflow_activities.action: Aggregate a subsystem-level block DSM, fold it along the diagonal, take reciprocal connection strengths, and fill missing pair distances with shortest paths to calculate coupling.
workflow_activities.decision_rules: Use the minimum weighted path, which need not have the fewest subsystem hops.
workflow_activities.quality_or_exit_checks: Every subsystem pair receives a direct or shortest-path distance where connected.

workflow_activities.action: Convert each subsystem DSM to Boolean form, add identity links, and repeatedly multiply it until transitive closure converges to calculate cohesion paths.
workflow_activities.decision_rules: Convergence occurs when P^n equals P^(n-1).
workflow_activities.quality_or_exit_checks: Boolean multiplication reaches convergence and output-function paths are counted.
workflow_activities.branching_iteration_or_rework: Repeat multiplication until convergence for each subsystem.

workflow_activities.action: Substitute the scale, cyclomatic, coupling, cohesion, interface, and partner values into the subsystem and system complexity equations and output the results.
workflow_activities.quality_or_exit_checks: A complexity value is produced for every subsystem and the whole system.

citations.quote: CubeSats, which were developed at educational institutions, often exhibit low mission success rates because of their limited design and system engineering experience. To address this issue, this study proposes a mission assurance framework that integrates system complexity evaluation with component importance analysis using the design structure matrix.

Within this framework, system configuration and dependencies among components visualized through design structure matrix (DSM) and complexity calculations, previously performed manually, are automated.
The proposed method was validated through a case study involving the BIRDS bus developed at the Kyushu Institute of Technology.

The results demonstrate that DSM-based system reconfiguration can reduce system complexity by more than 80% at the highest mission success level while improving the distribution of critical functions.

This framework provides an effective tool for assessing design validity from multiple perspectives during the early development phase prior to the preliminary design review. This approach is expected to increase the reliability and mission success rates of student CubeSat projects.

This study reformulated the existing complexity calculation workflow into a DSM-based representation to enable reproducible and consistent evaluation of system complexity during iterative architecture updates.
In addition, in-house software was developed to compute the complexity directly from the DSM, eliminating the manual counting and pathfinding required in the conventional method.
Finally, the resulting complexity metrics were incorporated into the repeatable mission assurance framework, demonstrating that they can guide specific architecture modifications.

By providing a repeatable and scalable approach to complexity-informed design decision-making, this work offers a practical tool for strengthening mission assurance and improving the success rates of CubeSat missions.
The DSM is a network modeling tool that represents the components forming a system and their interactions, thereby clarifying the system architecture [21].

A cell at row i and column j indicates that the component j output something to component i. Therefore, the matrix columns represent the providing (output) side, whereas the rows correspond to the receiving (input) side.
This research utilized the DSM to automate these sequences. This chapter shows the flow of calculating the complexity of the satellite system using the DSM step by step using an original DSM.

In this study, the algorithm is applied to each subsystem-level DSM to evaluate reachability among components and to determine, for each component, the set of components that can be reached from it via a directed path.

The ISM essentially computes the transitive closure within the subsystem graph (see Appendix B) [23, 32]. By multiplying the Boolean matrix in the ISM method, invisible indirect connections can be revealed when this method is applied to an entire subsystem.

The results show no significant discrepancies between the manual and automated calculations, demonstrating that the proposed method and software are both functional and effective for large-scale analysis. A minor discrepancy of approximately one was occasionally observed, which is attributed to cumulative rounding errors in the manual workflow.
The DSM-based automatic calculation software requires the DSM model created in the Excel file and the number of parts that make up each subsystem.

Model creation and data entry are required in both cases. The key difference is that the DSM-based tool automates the calculation step, whereas the WDM-based workflow relies on manual counting and path tracing.

On the basis of these results, optimal system designs with reduced complexity can be explored by iteratively modifying the DSM, such as by replacing, removing, or adding rows and columns, to minimize overall complexity.

Thus, reducing system complexity does not necessarily guarantee higher mission success. A careful trade-off must be made between the probability of failure and the severity of its potential impact.

In the proposed framework, the required functions and the associated importance of components are mapped on the DSM under progressively defined mission success levels to identify systematic bottlenecks and design imbalances as a first step. On the basis of this original DSM, DSMs are generated to correspond with each defined mission success level, and the complexity of each is calculated.

To reduce system complexity, the DSM structure is refined by addressing system imbalances. Specifically, clusters are reorganized, and interfaces are simplified through operations such as merging, splitting, and reordering rows and columns.

The objective is to derive a configuration that minimizes overall system complexity while preserving the functionality necessary to meet mission requirements. This framework is intended for application before the preliminary design review (PDR) phase, when the system configuration is nearly finalized.

Between 2015 and 2023, a total of 17 CubeSats were developed across six generations, with an additional CubeSat project scheduled for 2025 [35-39]. As a result, all phases of the CubeSat project, including mission planning, design, testing, and satellite operation, must be completed within a 2-year period.
